items.name: 153 premium / limited-edition ballpoint
items.tagline: Korea's ₩300 everyday pen, reborn in metal.
story: Every Korean has held a Monami 153. Launched in 1963 as the country's first domestic ballpoint, the white-and-black hexagonal pen became the default pen of classrooms, banks and offices — and still sells for a few hundred won.

Since 2014 Monami has been re-issuing the 153 as a premium object: brass, aluminium and lacquered bodies, seasonal colours, and collaborations that sell out within hours of release. The shape is unchanged, the click is the same, but the weight in the hand is a different thing entirely. It's the gift that makes Koreans smile with recognition.

items.name: Q-Knock gel pen
items.tagline: The pen every Korean student has in their bag.
story: Dong-A's Q-Knock is the quiet best-seller of Korean stationery: a retractable gel pen with a soft grip, a clean quick-drying line and a price so low you buy them by the box. It's the pen that fills exam halls and office drawers across the country.

What makes it loved is consistency — the same smooth line from the first page to the last, in a 0.4 mm that suits Hangul's tight strokes. Refills are everywhere, and the colour range runs well beyond black and blue.

items.name: 6-hole binder planner (A5 / A6 wide)
items.tagline: The planner you build yourself.
story: In 2026 the Korean planner trend swung away from bound yearly diaries toward refillable 6-ring binders. The appeal is control: pick the cover, choose weekly or daily inserts, add dot-grid pages for notes, swap sections as the year changes.

Paperian and ICONIC lead the category with soft PU and vegan-leather covers in muted colours, and a deep ecosystem of inserts, dividers and pockets. The A6-wide format — slightly wider than A6 so the rings don't eat the page — is the Korean favourite.

items.name: Index tabs & sticky notes
items.tagline: The organising layer for your binder.
story: Plepic makes the small pieces that make a planner work: translucent index tabs, slim sticky flags, minimal pastel notes. They're thin enough not to bulk up a binder and quiet enough not to shout over your handwriting.

Koreans buy them in sets — one for colour-coding subjects, one for marking book pages, one for the fridge. The design language is restrained, which is exactly why they pair with every planner on this list.

items.name: Botanical leaf sticky notes
items.tagline: Sticky notes shaped like real leaves.
story: Appree's leaf notes are a small Korean design classic: die-cut sticky notes printed as ginkgo, maple, birch and other leaves, realistic enough that a desk covered in them looks like autumn arrived indoors.
They've been a gift-shop staple for over a decade and are one of the most-exported Korean stationery items. Use them as bookmarks, labels or just to leave a nicer note.

items.name: Planner sticker packs
items.tagline: 다꾸 — decorating your diary is a daily ritual.
story: 다꾸 (dakku, "diary decorating") is a full-blown adult hobby in Korea: journaling every day and decorating the page with stickers, tapes and tiny illustrations. Sticker packs from Suatelier, Dailylike and NACOO are the raw material.
Expect transparent and matte sheets, tiny food and animal illustrations, weather icons, mood faces, and themed seasonal packs. They're cheap, so people collect by the dozen.

items.name: Literature-inspired fountain pen ink
items.tagline: Ink colours named after novels and planets.
story: Two Korean ink makers went global in the last few years. Wearingeul (글입다, "wearing text") bottles colours inspired by literature — a muted blue for a Yun Dong-ju poem, a dusty rose for The Little Prince — each with a shimmer or sheen chosen to match the story. Colorverse names its inks after space: nebulae, moons, missions.
Both are small-batch, beautifully packaged and loved by fountain-pen communities worldwide. A bottle is the ideal gift for anyone who writes by hand.

items.name: Washi / masking tape sets
items.tagline: Cheap, giftable, endlessly collectible.
story: Masking tape is the glue of Korean diary culture — literally. Dailylike's fabric-inspired patterns and ICONIC's minimal lines come in slim 10–15 mm rolls that tear by hand, write-on-able with a pen, and lift off without damaging paper.
Sets of three to five coordinated rolls are how most people buy them: one floral, one grid, one plain colour. They end up on planners, gift wrap, laptops and fridge notes.

items.name: Reading journal & bookmarks
items.tagline: Text-hip: reading is cool again.
story: "텍스트힙" (text-hip) is the Korean term for the return of reading as a lifestyle — visible in bookshop cafés, reading clubs and a boom in book accessories. A reading journal gives each book a page: title, dates, rating, favourite lines.

ICONIC's journals are slim and tidy; Kyobo Hottracks, the bookshop chain's own goods line, pairs them with metal and leather bookmarks. Together they're the fastest-growing niche in Korean stationery.

story: Artbox runs more than 300 stores across Korea, and its own-brand character goods are what fill the baskets: sticker packs, pen pouches, memo pads and desk trays featuring its house characters and seasonal collaborations.

It's affordable gift culture at scale — the shop you duck into for a ₩2,000 sticker pack and leave with a bag. For visitors it's the single easiest place to see what Korean stationery looks like right now.

items.name: Beginner knitting / crochet kit
items.tagline: Korea's #1 healing hobby, in one box.
story: 뜨개 (knitting and crochet) became the defining slow hobby of young Koreans in the mid-2020s: offline, screen-free, and with a finished object at the end to photograph. Kits removed the barrier — yarn, hook or needles, pattern and sometimes a video lesson in one package.
Typical first projects are a small bag, a scrunchie, a coaster set or a plush keyring. Dongdaemun's yarn market and Naver Smart Store sellers supply hundreds of variations.

Tufting — the powered big-brother for rugs — exploded through Korean workshops; starter kits bring the small-scale version home.

It's where Korea's book culture and its craft boom overlap — the perfect gift for a reader who already has every book.

It's low-cost, quiet and oddly meditative, which is why it keeps showing up in Korean 'healing hobby' lists.
